author: EmuCore - Hub
title: Dump and verify your own PlayStation 2 BIOS
summary: A legality-first BIOS workflow using a personally owned console, the official PCSX2 biosdrain guidance, two independent dumps, hashes, recovery steps, and checks that avoid sharing proprietary firmware.
heroAlt: Bottom side of a PlayStation 2 Slim motherboard showing the console hardware that contains its firmware

blocks.text: A PlayStation 2 BIOS is proprietary Sony firmware. Use a dump made from a console that you own, keep it private, and do not download, upload, trade or bundle BIOS files with an emulator. The official PCSX2 guide recommends biosdrain and documents supported ways to launch it. This manual begins after you have chosen a lawful homebrew launch method appropriate for your own console; it does not cover hardware circumvention or obtaining someone else's firmware.

items: A personally owned PlayStation 2 in reliable working order.
The current biosdrain.elf obtained from the official F0bes/biosdrain release page.
A homebrew launch path described by the official PCSX2 BIOS guide, such as an existing FreeMcBoot setup.
A small, known-good USB 2.0 flash drive partitioned as MBR and formatted FAT32, with every valuable file backed up first.
A computer with enough space for two dumps and a hashing tool such as PowerShell Get-FileHash, sha256sum or shasum.

blocks.text: Formatting a drive destroys its existing contents. Verify the selected physical device by capacity and label before formatting. Never use a command copied from a guide until the target drive has been checked.

items: 1. Download biosdrain only from the official project and copy biosdrain.elf to the FAT32 USB drive.
2. Safely eject the USB drive, connect it to the PS2, and start the console through your established homebrew launcher.
3. Open uLaunchELF, enter mass:, and run biosdrain.elf. Do not power off the console or remove the drive while data is being written.
4. Wait for biosdrain to report Finished Everything. Return to uLaunchELF or shut down normally, then remove the USB drive.
5. On the computer, copy the complete output set into a new read-only archive folder named for the console model and the dump date. Preserve the original filenames.

blocks.text: The output can include the main ROM plus companion files such as ROM1, ROM2, NVM or MEC data, depending on console model and dumper behavior. EmuCoreX normally needs the main BIOS image, but the companion files are useful preservation evidence and should remain with the private master copy. Do not rename every component to .bin or concatenate files: a filename extension does not repair an incomplete dump.
Verify with a second independent read

items: 1. Power-cycle the PS2 and repeat the dump into a different empty folder; do not overwrite the first set.
2. Compare file counts and exact byte sizes between the two folders.
3. Calculate SHA-256 for each corresponding file. On Windows, run Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 against each private copy; on Linux use sha256sum, and on macOS use shasum -a 256.
4. Accept the dump only when the paired files have identical hashes. Store the hashes in a small text manifest beside the private master copy.
5. Copy only the verified main BIOS image to the Android device and select it through EmuCoreX's Choose BIOS File action.

blocks.text: A matching pair proves that the same bytes were read twice; it does not authorize sharing the file and it does not prove that an unrelated web hash belongs to your console. Model and region information should be read by the emulator from the verified image. Avoid online hash lists of unknown provenance, and never modify the dump to force a different region. If a modchip is installed, follow the PCSX2 warning about disabling it for the biosdrain run because an active chip can cause an incomplete or corrupted result.

After selection, the setup or Settings screen should mark the BIOS as ready. Launch BIOS from the drawer before testing a game: the system menu should render, accept controller input and retain its language or clock data after a normal exit. Then cold-start one personally dumped game. A failure here is more useful than a random compatibility test because the two-copy hash check has already removed unstable USB reads from the investigation.

items: If the two hashes differ, discard neither copy immediately. Reformat or replace the USB drive, repeat two new dumps, and keep the earlier sets quarantined for comparison.
If mass: is empty, try a smaller or older USB 2.0 drive; PS2 USB homebrew can be selective even when a modern computer reads the device.
If biosdrain never reaches its completion message, power down only after write activity has stopped, then verify the launcher method and obtain a fresh official biosdrain.elf.
If EmuCoreX reports Files not found, reselect the verified main image through Android's document picker and keep it in a stable local folder.
If BIOS boot works but one game fails, preserve the verified dump and troubleshoot the game, renderer or per-game profile instead of replacing firmware at random.

blocks.text: Keep one offline backup of the verified dump set and its SHA-256 manifest on storage you control. Encrypt that backup if other people can access the device. The Android working copy may be replaced after a storage move, but the private master and its hashes should remain unchanged. This gives you a recoverable, auditable BIOS source without turning proprietary firmware into distributable content.
Read the official PCSX2 BIOS-dumping guide before starting
